steps.prompt: What does the to + verb mean here?
options: It gives the reason — why the person did it.
It is part of the main verb of the sentence.
It shows that the action is in the future.
steps.answer: It gives the reason — why the person did it.
steps.why: This is the infinitive of purpose. It answers Why?

steps.title: Uses of the infinitive with to
steps.html:
PatternExample
to give a reasonI spoke to an architect to find out more.
after my job / my role isMy job is to advise clients.
after certain verbsThey decided to move the desks.
after it’s + adjectiveIt’s important to show what you have finished.
in order to (formal)They moved the desks in order to encourage communication.
for + nounI went there for a meeting.
for + -ing (what a thing is for)This room is for having informal meetings.

The commonest way to say why is simply to + base form: I called to ask about the job.

Never use for + base form: say I came here to study, not for study.

Use for + a noun: I came here for a meeting. Use for + -ing when you describe what a thing is used for: a room for having meetings.

In order to means the same as to but sounds formal. In speech, plain to is normal.

After it’s + an adjective, use to + base form: It’s important to ask. It’s difficult to train somebody remotely.

You met You use it to … in Lesson 15, when you explained a word. This is the same structure.

steps.title: What a job involves now
steps.html:
Ten years ago almost nobody in Europe worked from home. Then, very quickly, millions of people had to. Today about one worker in four in the European Union is remote or hybrid — at home for part of the week, in the office for the rest. Some companies have worked this way for five years now and say they will not go back. Companies that used to measure a working day in hours try to measure it in results instead.

The job titles have not changed much, but the day-to-day work has. A manager’s first task used to be to watch the room. Now it is to write things down. “My job is to make the work visible,” says Priya Menon, who has led a hybrid team in Bengaluru since 2020. “If nobody can see you, somebody has to explain in detail what everyone is doing.” That means more paperwork, not less: reports, notes, and a short written answer to every enquiry.

Not everything is better. It is harder to train a new candidate when the team is in five places. Managers say it takes longer to recruit, and much longer to know whether the new person is any good. But productivity has not fallen. In most studies it has stayed the same or risen slightly, and workers say the same three things: they are less often in a hurry, their week is more flexible, and they are no longer in trouble for arriving ten minutes late.

One warning sits under all of this. The people who do best in a hybrid team already knew everybody before the team split up. For a new candidate, the first six months are much harder than they used to be, and no amount of paperwork fixes that.

Sources. Written for this course from public research: Eurofound, Living and working in the EU (telework series) · Eurostat, employed persons working from home · Bloom, Han & Liang (2024), Nature 630, on hybrid work and productivity. Figures are rounded. Priya Menon is a composite manager written for this course; no words are attributed to a real person.

Not everything is better. It is harder to train a new candidate when the team is in five places. Managers say it takes longer to recruit, and much longer to know whether the new person is any good. But productivity has not fallen. In most studies it has stayed the same or risen slightly, and workers say the same three things: they are less often in a hurry, their week is more flexible, and they are no longer in trouble for arriving ten minutes late.

One warning sits under all of this. The people who do best in a hybrid team already knew everybody before the team split up. For a new candidate, the first six months are much harder than they used to be, and no amount of paperwork fixes that.
